Introduction

Diabetes, a chronic metabolic disorder (Disease code: diabetes), is primarily characterized by impaired glucose homeostasis due to deficient insulin secretion, impaired insulin action, or both. This condition leads to persistent hyperglycemia and subsequent multisystem tissue injury. Beyond glucose dysregulation, diabetes involves complex biological alterations, including vascular injury, chronic inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and tissue-specific stress responses. In an extensive analysis of the UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project data, we identified 880 plasma proteins significantly associated with diabetes. This analysis was conducted on a cohort comprising 47,912 controls and 3,787 cases, with significance determined using Bonferroni correction at a stringent threshold of P < 0.000000001. The identification of these proteins is crucial for unraveling the molecular mechanisms underlying diabetes, which is known for its heterogeneity and complex progression. Understanding these proteins can provide insights into potential diagnostic markers and therapeutic targets. To further explore the functional implications of these proteins, we conducted a comprehensive functional enrichment analysis using multiple pathway databases, including Gene Ontology Molecular Function, Gene Ontology Biological Process, Gene Ontology Cellular Component, Reactome, and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG). This analysis revealed 105 significantly enriched biological pathways, highlighting key processes such as innate immune activation, cytokine-linked signaling, complement biology, neutrophil degranulation, extracellular matrix organization, and vasculature development. Among the most notable pathways were neutrophil degranulation, with 88 associated proteins (P = 2.95 × 10−19), regulation of vasculature development with 50 proteins (P = 4.18 × 10−16), and extracellular matrix organization with 59 proteins (P = 4.90 × 10−14). These pathways underscore the complex systems-level network that supports diabetes, integrating immune dysregulation, vascular remodeling, and altered nutrient sensing. Literature evidence further corroborates these findings, with 164 distinct PubMed references supporting the involvement of top-ranked proteins such as CTSD, CEACAM1, and CD36 in these pathways. The STRING protein-protein interaction network analysis retained 92 high-confidence edges among 48 proteins, with a mean interaction score of 0.89. Key hub proteins, including ITGAM, ITGB2, and PTPRC, emerged as central nodes, suggesting coordinated interaction neighborhoods that complement the enrichment analysis. This network topology provides a deeper understanding of how these proteins interact within the broader biological framework of diabetes. In the following sections, we will delve into the detailed analysis of significant pathways and molecular interactions, offering a comprehensive view of the biological underpinnings of diabetes. [323] [324] [325] [326] [327] [328]

    Drug/pathway-level therapeutic context

    • Inflammation, cytokine signaling, and immune regulation
      pathways: Viral protein interaction with cytokine and cytokine receptor, Neutrophil degranulation, Complement system; candidate proteins: C3, CR1
      This axis can support inflammation-focused target validation and comparison with immune-modulating therapeutic contexts when the disease setting makes that clinically relevant.
    • Neuroimmune, synaptic, and neuronal signaling
      pathways: regulation of vasculature development
      This axis provides a pathway-level context for neuronal or neuroimmune mechanisms, but it does not by itself identify a neuropsychiatric or neurologic treatment strategy.
    • Vascular remodeling, extracellular matrix, and tissue structure
      pathways: Extracellular matrix organization, Neutrophil degranulation, regulation of vasculature development, Pluripotent stem cell differentiation pathway
      This axis can help interpret remodeling, vascular, or matrix-related disease biology and can prioritize follow-up assays around tissue-level mechanisms.
    • Metabolic, lipid, endocrine, and stress-response biology
      pathways: lipid localization, Neutrophil degranulation, regulation of vasculature development, Complement system
      This axis can place candidate proteins into metabolic or endocrine-stress contexts, which is useful for hypothesis generation and guideline-aware comparison without implying medication choice.
    • Cell trafficking, secretion, endoplasmic-reticulum biology, and proteostasis
      pathways: Lysosome, Pluripotent stem cell differentiation pathway
      This axis highlights cell-state and protein-handling mechanisms that may explain why circulating protein signals converge across multiple pathways.

    Clinical-practice caution

    BioInsight provides hypothesis-generation support only. The drug and pathway annotations summarize retained statistical, literature, pathway, DGIdb, and network evidence; they do not constitute clinical treatment recommendations, prescribing guidance, or proof of efficacy. Any guideline discussion should be read as contextual comparison with clinical-practice literature, not as a recommendation to use or avoid a therapy.

    5. Neutrophil degranulation (REAC:R-HSA-6798695)

    Agent Summary: Neutrophil degranulation is a crucial component of innate immunity where neutrophils release antimicrobial and inflammatory mediators, which can be beneficial for pathogen defense but harmful when dysregulated. Pathway members (enrichment overlap): ACAA1, ADA2, ADAM8, ADGRE5, AHSG, ANPEP. [323] [324] [325]
    Read Context ▽

    Neutrophil degranulation is a core effector program of innate immunity in which neutrophils release preformed antimicrobial and inflammatory mediators from intracellular granules into phagosomes or the extracellular space after activation. This process is tightly coordinated with neutrophil adhesion, migration, phagocytosis, oxidative burst, cytoskeletal remodeling, and, under some conditions, extracellular trap formation. The released cargo includes proteases, oxidant-generating enzymes, alarmins, matrix-remodeling proteins, and iron-binding proteins, such as myeloperoxidase, neutrophil elastase, matrix metalloproteinase eight, matrix metalloproteinase nine, lactoferrin, and other granule-associated molecules. Physiologically, degranulation contributes to rapid pathogen killing and orchestration of downstream immune responses. However, when excessive, chronic, spatially misdirected, or metabolically dysregulated, it can damage host tissues, amplify sterile inflammation, promote endothelial dysfunction, alter extracellular matrix turnover, and facilitate thrombosis. Because diabetes is characterized by hyperglycemia, altered cellular metabolism, oxidative stress, low-grade inflammation, vascular injury, and impaired host defense, neutrophil degranulation is highly relevant to disease initiation, progression, and complications. In this context, the pathway is perhaps best viewed as a double-edged process: it may be functionally defective in antimicrobial defense while simultaneously contributing to chronic inflammatory tissue injury in metabolic organs and the vasculature.

    Against this biological background, the collected literature indicates that neutrophil degranulation is closely linked to diabetes across both autoimmune and metabolic forms of the disease, as well as across several major complications. In type two diabetes, clinical evidence shows that circulating biomarkers of neutrophil degranulation, including myeloperoxidase, resistin, matrix metalloproteinase eight, and the matrix metalloproteinase nine and tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases one complex, are associated particularly with the restrictive echocardiographic pattern and diastolic dysfunction, supporting a role for neutrophil-derived inflammatory and matrix-remodeling mediators in diabetic cardiomyopathy and myocardial stiffness rather than merely reflecting generalized inflammation alone [323]. Mechanistically, hyperglycemia appears to reprogram neutrophil signaling and activation states: phosphoproteomic profiling demonstrated that high glucose activates distinct kinase networks linked to neutrophil functional responses, while homocysteine preferentially induced signaling associated with neutrophil degranulation and cytoskeletal remodeling, suggesting that the metabolic environment of diabetes directly shapes degranulation-related pathways and may bias neutrophils toward pathogenic inflammatory outputs [324]. At the same time, older functional work emphasized that diabetes can impair multiple neutrophil activities, including chemotaxis, phagocytosis, microbicidal capacity, migration, reactive oxygen species production, and cytokine release, indicating that diabetic neutrophils may exist in a paradoxical state in which host-defense functions are blunted whereas injurious inflammatory programs remain aberrantly activated or misdirected [325]. In type one diabetes, several studies support participation of neutrophil degranulation in autoimmune pathogenesis: review evidence indicates that neutrophil-derived cytotoxic granule products, reactive oxygen species, cytokines, and extracellular traps can injure pancreatic beta cells and amplify diabetogenic immune responses, while systems and transcriptomic studies further identify neutrophil degranulation among the immune pathways associated with type one diabetes biology and heterogeneity of beta-cell decline after diagnosis [326] [327] [328]. Beyond primary disease mechanisms, neutrophil degranulation also appears to contribute to diabetic complications. A recent review on extracellular traps in diabetes highlighted that neutrophil granule constituents such as myeloperoxidase and neutrophil elastase participate in inflammatory tissue injury, thrombosis, impaired wound healing, retinopathy, stroke, and coronary artery disease, linking degranulation to the broader spectrum of vascular and reparative dysfunction in diabetes [329]. Consistently, bioinformatic analysis of diabetes-related stroke identified granulin precursor as a hub gene connected to neutrophil extracellular trap formation through neutrophil degranulation, suggesting that this pathway may connect diabetes to heightened thromboinflammatory cerebrovascular risk [330]. Additional human studies reinforce the biomarker potential of this pathway, including elevated plasma lactoferrin, a neutrophil degranulation product, in type two diabetes with dry eye disease, where lactoferrin correlated with glycosylated hemoglobin, implying a relationship between glycemic burden and degranulation-associated inflammation [331]. Finally, intervention-related observations are compatible with a pathogenic role of neutrophil activation in metabolic disease, as lower neutrophil counts were associated with a greater likelihood of remission of type two diabetes during Mediterranean dietary intervention, indirectly supporting the concept that attenuation of neutrophil-driven inflammatory programs may accompany metabolic improvement [332]. Taken together, the available evidence supports neutrophil degranulation as a biologically plausible and clinically relevant pathway in diabetes, linking hyperglycemia and metabolic stress to innate immune dysregulation, pancreatic beta-cell injury, cardiovascular remodeling, thromboinflammation, mucosal and ocular inflammation, and impaired tissue repair. [323] [324] [325] [326] [327] [328] [329] [330] [331] [332]

    To complement this pathway-level interpretation, the network analysis below illustrates how these 88 proteins are connected at the protein-protein interaction level.

    The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network of these 88 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for interactive inspection of the network topology and functional connectivity.

    During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following. ACAA1 is notable in the context of diabetes because altered lipid handling is a central feature of insulin resistance, hepatic steatosis, and lipotoxicity. By participating in peroxisomal beta-oxidation, ACAA1 contributes to the breakdown of very-long-chain and other fatty acyl-CoAs that cannot be managed efficiently by mitochondria alone. Impaired peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation can promote intracellular lipid accumulation and oxidative stress, both of which are mechanistically linked to reduced insulin responsiveness in liver and other metabolic tissues. Thus, ACAA1 stands out as a metabolically relevant protein whose function intersects directly with the dysregulated fatty acid flux that characterizes type 2 diabetes and related metabolic syndrome states. [333] [334]

    In a related metabolic-regulatory context, ADA2 points toward neuroendocrine control of glucose homeostasis. ADA2 is potentially relevant to diabetes because adrenergic signaling is an important regulator of glucose homeostasis, insulin secretion, and counter-regulatory stress responses. Inhibition of adenylate cyclase reduces cyclic adenosine monophosphate signaling, a pathway that strongly influences hormone secretion and metabolic adaptation. In pancreatic islets, alpha-2 adrenergic signaling is well known to suppress insulin release, and excessive sympathetic tone can therefore contribute to impaired glycemic control. Although the present annotation is concise, the receptor's core function places it within a biologically plausible axis linking neuroendocrine stress signaling to beta-cell dysfunction and hyperglycemia.

    Shifting from neuroendocrine regulation to innate immune signaling, BST2 may be relevant because diabetes is frequently accompanied by chronic inflammatory activation. BST2 is relevant to diabetes primarily through the intersection of innate immunity, chronic inflammation, and interferon signaling. Low-grade inflammatory activation is a hallmark of type 2 diabetes, while type 1 diabetes is strongly shaped by antiviral and interferon-related immune pathways. BST2 is particularly interesting because it is both an antiviral effector and an immunomodulatory molecule capable of influencing nuclear factor kappa B signaling and dendritic cell interferon responses. These properties make it a plausible contributor to inflammatory tissue stress, including in pancreatic islets or adipose tissue, where persistent innate immune activation can worsen insulin resistance or beta-cell injury. Its broad immune-regulatory profile therefore gives BST2 potential relevance to diabetes pathogenesis, especially in settings where viral triggers or interferon signatures are implicated. [335] [336] [337] [338] [339] [340] [341] [342] [343] [344] [345] [346] [347] [348] [349] [350] [351] [352] [353] [354]

    Extending this theme of innate immune activation, CD14 may be one of the more direct links between inflammatory sensing and metabolic dysfunction. CD14 is one of the most compelling diabetes-related proteins in this list because it sits at the center of innate immune sensing and metabolic inflammation. Activation of the CD14-TLR4 axis by endotoxin or other inflammatory ligands promotes nuclear factor kappa B signaling and cytokine production, processes strongly implicated in insulin resistance, adipose tissue inflammation, and beta-cell stress. The relevance is particularly high for type 2 diabetes, where metabolic endotoxemia and chronic activation of innate immunity have been proposed to drive systemic insulin resistance. CD14 also binds electronegative low-density lipoprotein, linking inflammatory signaling with dyslipidemia, another major component of diabetic pathology. Overall, CD14 represents a mechanistic bridge between microbial products, sterile inflammation, lipid abnormalities, and impaired glucose metabolism. [355] [356] [357] [358]

    In parallel, CD300A may be relevant because inhibitory immune checkpoints can shape the amplitude of chronic metabolic inflammation. CD300A is relevant to diabetes because it functions as a brake on innate immune activation, especially on MYD88-dependent toll-like receptor signaling. Since chronic low-grade inflammation is a major driver of insulin resistance and tissue dysfunction in type 2 diabetes, inhibitory receptors such as CD300A may influence the threshold and duration of inflammatory responses in metabolic tissues. By restraining toll-like receptor signaling, CD300A could theoretically mitigate cytokine production and immune-mediated damage. This is particularly important because excessive innate immune activation in adipose tissue, liver, and pancreatic islets contributes to metabolic deterioration. Therefore, CD300A stands out as a potential endogenous counter-regulatory factor in diabetes-associated inflammation. [359] [360] [361]

    Moving from inflammatory control to tissue remodeling and survival signaling, CHI3L1 may also have potential relevance. CHI3L1 is highly relevant to diabetes because it combines inflammatory, remodeling, and survival-related functions that map closely onto diabetic complications and metabolic tissue dysfunction. Its ability to regulate macrophage differentiation, dendritic cell accumulation, and inflammatory cytokine pathways suggests a role in the chronic immune activation observed in obesity and type 2 diabetes. Moreover, its involvement in AKT1 signaling is particularly notable, as AKT is a central node in insulin signaling and cellular survival pathways. CHI3L1 may therefore influence both inflammatory tone and tissue adaptation in organs commonly affected by diabetes, including adipose tissue, vasculature, gut, and lung. This makes it a strong candidate for relevance not only to metabolic dysregulation but also to fibrosis, repair, and chronic complications.

    A more indirect but still potentially meaningful connection to diabetic tissue stress may be seen with CKAP4. CKAP4 has a more indirect but still potentially meaningful connection to diabetes through regulation of cell growth and stress signaling. Diabetes is associated with altered epithelial integrity, impaired repair responses, and abnormal proliferative control in several tissues, including kidney and vasculature. A receptor that mediates antiproliferative signaling could therefore influence tissue remodeling or regenerative capacity under diabetic stress. Although the current annotation does not directly place CKAP4 in a metabolic pathway, its role in cell-surface signaling and proliferation control may be relevant in the context of diabetic complications characterized by epithelial dysfunction.

    Continuing toward proteins that may amplify inflammatory effector damage, CTSC is of particular interest. CTSC is of interest for diabetes because it amplifies protease networks involved in inflammation and immune-cell effector function. By activating elastase, cathepsin G, and granzymes, CTSC can contribute to tissue injury, extracellular matrix remodeling, and immune-mediated cytotoxicity. These processes are relevant to diabetic inflammation, vascular injury, and potentially beta-cell damage in autoimmune contexts. In type 2 diabetes, neutrophil and myeloid protease activity has been linked to chronic inflammatory tissue remodeling, whereas in type 1 diabetes, granzyme-related pathways may influence immune destruction of beta cells. CTSC therefore represents a plausible upstream regulator of damaging proteolytic cascades in diabetes-associated pathology. [362] [363]

    At the level of intracellular proteostasis, ERP44 may be relevant because beta-cell function depends heavily on endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis. ERP44 is particularly relevant to diabetes because endoplasmic reticulum stress, oxidative protein folding, and calcium homeostasis are all central determinants of beta-cell health and insulin secretory capacity. Pancreatic beta cells are highly dependent on efficient endoplasmic reticulum function to fold and process insulin, and disturbances in endoplasmic reticulum redox balance can trigger the unfolded protein response and apoptosis. ERP44 also regulates ITPR1-mediated calcium flux, a key factor in stimulus-secretion coupling and cell survival. For these reasons, ERP44 stands out as a strong mechanistic candidate linking proteostasis stress to beta-cell dysfunction and progressive diabetes. [364] [365] [366] [367]

    Within this same metabolic-stress framework, FGR appears especially notable because its annotated functions intersect directly with insulin action. FGR is one of the strongest diabetes-relevant proteins in this dataset because its annotated functions directly involve insulin action, glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis, and hepatic endoplasmic reticulum stress adaptation. These are core biological processes disrupted in type 2 diabetes. The annotation explicitly states that FGR is necessary for insulin-stimulated increases in glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis, indicating a direct role in insulin sensitivity. In addition, its promotion of XBP1 nuclear translocation during metabolic overloading suggests that FGR may help coordinate adaptive unfolded protein response signaling in the liver, thereby influencing glucose tolerance. This combination of insulin signaling and endoplasmic reticulum stress regulation makes FGR especially important for understanding mechanisms of metabolic dysfunction. [368] [369] [370] [371]

    A more indirect metabolic contribution may be considered for GGH through one-carbon metabolism and vascular biology. GGH may be relevant to diabetes through one-carbon metabolism, folate handling, and downstream effects on vascular health. Folate metabolism influences methylation pathways, homocysteine balance, and cellular proliferation, all of which can shape cardiometabolic risk and diabetic complications. Although GGH is not a canonical diabetes gene, altered folate metabolism may affect endothelial function and inflammation, potentially modifying susceptibility to microvascular and macrovascular disease in diabetes. Its role is therefore likely indirect but biologically plausible, especially in relation to complication risk. [372] [373]

    By contrast, GPI has a more central relationship to glucose handling itself. GPI is highly relevant to diabetes because it occupies a central position in glucose metabolism. As a glycolytic enzyme, it contributes directly to intracellular glucose utilization, and disturbances in glycolytic flux are fundamental to both insulin resistance and beta-cell dysfunction. Its extracellular cytokine-like functions further broaden its significance, suggesting additional roles in angiogenesis, immune signaling, and tissue adaptation. These noncanonical functions are especially interesting in diabetes, a disease characterized not only by disordered glucose metabolism but also by vascular remodeling and chronic inflammation. GPI therefore stands out as a multifunctional protein linking core carbohydrate metabolism with systemic disease processes. [374] [375] [376] [377]

    Returning to immune restraint, LAIR1 may be relevant as a broad suppressor of inflammatory signaling. LAIR1 is important in diabetes because it is a broad negative regulator of immune activation, cytokine production, and nuclear factor kappa B signaling. These features are highly relevant to both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. In type 1 diabetes, inhibitory receptors that constrain lymphocyte activation may influence autoimmune beta-cell destruction. In type 2 diabetes, suppression of inflammatory cytokines and nuclear factor kappa B activity may help limit the chronic innate and adaptive immune activation that contributes to insulin resistance. LAIR1 therefore stands out as a potentially protective immunoregulatory node whose reduced activity could favor persistent inflammation and tissue damage.

    At the level of intermediary metabolism, NIT2 may have a subtler but still plausible connection to diabetes-related metabolic flexibility. NIT2 is relevant to diabetes because it participates in intermediary metabolism and detoxification of potentially harmful nitrogen-containing metabolites. Its products, 2-oxoglutarate and oxaloacetate, are central metabolites in the tricarboxylic acid cycle and gluconeogenic pathways. Maintenance of these metabolic nodes is important in tissues with high energetic demand, including liver and pancreatic islets. While the connection to diabetes is less direct than for insulin signaling proteins, NIT2 may influence metabolic flexibility and cellular stress tolerance, both of which are impaired in diabetes. [378] [379]

    Lipid trafficking provides another important layer of diabetes biology, and NPC2 may be relevant within this context. NPC2 is highly pertinent to diabetes because cholesterol trafficking and lysosomal lipid handling are increasingly recognized as major determinants of insulin sensitivity, inflammation, and beta-cell function. Defective intracellular cholesterol export can promote lipotoxic stress, organelle dysfunction, and inflammatory activation. In pancreatic beta cells, excessive cholesterol accumulation impairs insulin secretion, while in macrophages and liver it contributes to metabolic inflammation and steatosis. NPC2 therefore stands out as a lipid-homeostasis factor with plausible relevance to multiple aspects of diabetes pathogenesis, including dyslipidemia and organelle stress. [58] [59] [60] [61]

    Shifting from intracellular lipid handling to vascular integrity, PTPRB may be relevant because endothelial dysfunction is a major feature of diabetic complications. PTPRB is relevant to diabetes chiefly because endothelial dysfunction is a defining feature of diabetic vascular disease. Maintenance of endothelial junction integrity, polarity, and vascular lumen architecture is essential for barrier function and microvascular health. In diabetes, chronic hyperglycemia, oxidative stress, and inflammation disrupt endothelial cohesion, thereby contributing to nephropathy, retinopathy, and cardiovascular complications. A protein that stabilizes endothelial organization may therefore be highly important in modulating susceptibility to diabetic microangiopathy and vascular leak. [380] [381] [382] [383] [384]

    Extracellular matrix remodeling represents another major component of chronic diabetic injury, which brings QSOX1 into consideration. QSOX1 is potentially important in diabetes because extracellular matrix remodeling and fibrosis are major components of diabetic complications. By promoting disulfide bond formation in extracellular proteins and supporting laminin incorporation into matrix, QSOX1 can influence tissue architecture, adhesion, and wound repair. These functions are especially relevant in diabetes, where impaired matrix organization contributes to poor wound healing, vascular basement membrane abnormalities, and fibrotic remodeling in organs such as kidney and heart. QSOX1 therefore stands out as a plausible contributor to structural tissue changes associated with chronic hyperglycemia. [385] [386] [387] [388] [389] [390]

    At the interface of innate immunity and mitochondrial biology, RNASET2 may also warrant attention. RNASET2 is relevant to diabetes because it links innate immune activation with mitochondrial ribonucleic acid homeostasis. The innate immune system has a major role in both autoimmune and metabolic forms of diabetes, and nucleic acid sensing pathways can drive inflammatory cytokine production. In addition, mitochondrial dysfunction is a key feature of insulin resistance and beta-cell failure. By participating in both ribonucleic acid sensing-related immunity and mitochondrial ribonucleic acid turnover, RNASET2 occupies an interesting intersection between inflammation and cellular energetics. This dual role makes it a plausible modifier of diabetes susceptibility or progression, particularly where sterile inflammation and mitochondrial stress coexist. [391] [392] [393] [394] [395]

    Another possible inflammatory link is provided by S100P through receptor for advanced glycation end products signaling. S100P is notable in diabetes because receptor for advanced glycation end products signaling is a well-established pathogenic pathway in hyperglycemia, advanced glycation end product biology, inflammation, and vascular damage. A protein capable of stimulating proliferation through receptor for advanced glycation end products may amplify inflammatory and remodeling responses in diabetic tissues. Its calcium-sensing properties are also relevant, given the importance of calcium signaling in insulin secretion and epithelial function. Thus, S100P may connect calcium-dependent signaling with receptor for advanced glycation end products-mediated inflammatory pathways that are central to diabetic complications, especially vascular and epithelial injury.

    Within the secretory pathway, SRP14 may be relevant because insulin biosynthesis depends on efficient protein targeting to the endoplasmic reticulum. SRP14 may be relevant to diabetes because efficient targeting of secretory proteins to the endoplasmic reticulum is essential for insulin biosynthesis and processing. Pancreatic beta cells are among the most secretory cell types in the body and are highly sensitive to defects in endoplasmic reticulum protein handling. Although SRP14 is a general secretory pathway component rather than a diabetes-specific factor, disruption of cotranslational targeting could aggravate endoplasmic reticulum stress and impair insulin production. Its significance therefore lies in the broader framework of beta-cell proteostasis. [396]

    Closely related to this theme, TXNDC5 may be especially important because insulin maturation depends on correct disulfide bond formation. TXNDC5 is strongly relevant to diabetes because it directly participates in endoplasmic reticulum protein folding and has documented activity toward insulin disulfide bonds. Proper disulfide bond formation is indispensable for insulin maturation, and endoplasmic reticulum oxidative folding defects are a major cause of beta-cell stress and failure. Given the extraordinary secretory burden placed on beta cells, proteins such as TXNDC5 may critically influence insulin biosynthesis, proinsulin processing quality, and susceptibility to unfolded protein response activation. This makes TXNDC5 a particularly compelling candidate in mechanisms linking endoplasmic reticulum dysfunction to diabetes. [397] [398]

    Mitochondrial dynamics and tissue repair add another dimension to diabetes complications, which may make VAT1 of interest. VAT1 is potentially relevant to diabetes through two disease-relevant processes: mitochondrial dynamics and wound repair. Mitochondrial fusion-fission balance is critical for insulin sensitivity, beta-cell function, and cellular stress adaptation, while impaired epidermal repair is a hallmark of diabetes-associated chronic wounds. Because VAT1 negatively regulates mitochondrial fusion and participates in calcium-regulated repair responses, it may influence both metabolic resilience and tissue healing. This makes it an interesting, though less established, candidate in the biology of diabetic complications.

    Finally, VNN1 may be relevant in the broader setting of redox balance and energy metabolism. VNN1 is relevant to diabetes because it influences coenzyme A precursor metabolism and generates cysteamine, a small thiol that can affect redox balance and inflammatory responses. Pantothenic acid recycling is tied to lipid and energy metabolism, while redox-active metabolites are important in oxidative stress, a major contributor to insulin resistance and diabetic tissue injury. Although the annotation is brief, VNN1's metabolic and redox-related functions make it a plausible participant in pathways that influence glucose-lipid homeostasis and chronic inflammation.

    6. regulation of vasculature development (GO:1901342)

    Agent Summary: The regulation of vasculature development is crucial for the formation and function of blood vessels, involving processes such as endothelial cell proliferation, migration, and angiocrine signaling. Pathway members (enrichment overlap): ADAM12, AMOT, ANGPTL3, ANGPTL4, ANGPTL7, BMPER. Context proteins (upstream regulators / disease context, not direct members): BMP4, BMP6, CTSD, TGFBR3. [280] [281] [282]
    Read Context ▽

    Regulation of vasculature development comprises all biological processes that increase, decrease, or otherwise shape the formation, patterning, maturation, and remodeling of blood vessels. This pathway includes endothelial cell proliferation, migration, sprouting, branching morphogenesis, lumen formation, recruitment of mural cells, stabilization of newly formed vessels, and tissue-specific angiocrine signaling that coordinates organ growth and metabolic function. Proper regulation is essential because both insufficient and excessive vessel formation can impair tissue oxygenation, nutrient delivery, endocrine exchange, and barrier integrity. In metabolic organs, especially pancreatic islets, retina, bone, placenta, heart, and brain, vascular development is not merely structural but also instructive, because developing vessels provide signals that influence cell differentiation, secretory capacity, and tissue homeostasis. The publications provided indicate that this pathway is governed by factors such as vascular endothelial growth factor A, hypoxia inducible factor signaling, endothelin one, adrenomedullin, renin angiotensin signaling, endothelial sirtuin pathways, and tissue-specific endothelial or paracrine regulators. In the context of diabetes, regulation of vasculature development spans early developmental programming, adaptive or maladaptive vascular remodeling during obesity and insulin resistance, and progressive microvascular injury that underlies complications such as diabetic retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, impaired wound healing, cognitive decline, placental dysfunction, and diabetic bone disease.

    Against this biological background, the collected literature suggests that regulation of vasculature development is closely intertwined with diabetes at both causal and consequence levels. First, altered vascular developmental programs can directly shape later glucose homeostasis. In pancreatic islets, beta two adrenergic receptor signaling restrains vascular endothelial growth factor A production during neonatal development; loss of this control causes excessive islet vascularization, defective insulin secretion, and adult glucose intolerance, suggesting that abnormal vessel growth during organogenesis can predispose to diabetes-relevant endocrine dysfunction [280]. Consistently, reviews on islet biology and transplantation emphasize that endothelial cells and islet vasculature are indispensable for endocrine maturation, survival, and function, further linking vascular developmental regulation to diabetes pathogenesis and therapy [281] [282]. Second, diabetes and obesity actively reprogram endothelial signaling pathways that control vascular remodeling. A particularly strong mechanistic study shows that endothelial FUN14 domain containing one is increased under diabetic conditions and promotes the obesity to type two diabetes transition through sirtuin three, GATA binding protein two, and endothelin one signaling, identifying the vascular endothelium as a potential driver of systemic metabolic deterioration rather than merely a passive target [283]. More broadly, diabetes is characterized by endothelial dysfunction, impaired nitric oxide bioavailability, oxidative stress, inflammation, and disturbed angiogenesis, all of which alter the frequency, rate, and quality of vessel growth and remodeling across tissues [284] [285] [286]. Third, dysregulated vascular development and remodeling contribute centrally to diabetic complications. In the retina, diabetes disrupts neurovascular regulation, promotes early vascular compromise, and ultimately drives capillary degeneration and pathological angiogenesis; protective roles for sirtuin one and microglial vascular regulation further indicate that altered control of vessel maintenance and remodeling is a key determinant of diabetic retinopathy progression [287] [288] [289]. In the brain, type two diabetes is linked to defective neurovascular coupling and microvascular pericyte pathology, providing a vascular developmental and remodeling framework for diabetes-associated cognitive decline and its overlap with neurodegeneration [290] [291]. In bone, type two diabetes related osteoporosis is associated with loss of specialized H type vessels, and restoration of Elabela apelin receptor signaling rescues angiogenesis osteogenesis coupling, indicating that diabetes may impair tissue specific vascular niche development with functional skeletal consequences [292]. Developmental exposure is also important: maternal diabetes perturbs cardiovascular and coronary vascular development in offspring, and gestational diabetes alters placental angiogenesis and vascular function, showing that diabetic environments can dysregulate vasculature development before birth with lasting effects on fetal oxygenation and cardiovascular risk [293] [294]. Finally, circulating vasoactive mediators such as adrenomedullin are elevated in diabetes and correlate with complications, supporting the concept that persistent diabetic metabolic stress shifts vascular growth and homeostatic signaling toward maladaptive remodeling [295]. Taken together, the evidence indicates that regulation of vasculature development is not peripheral to diabetes; rather, it appears to represent a core axis linking developmental programming, endothelial metabolic signaling, tissue specific vascular niche integrity, and the emergence of both systemic metabolic dysfunction and chronic diabetic complications. [280] [281] [282] [283] [284] [285] [286] [287] [288] [289] [290] [291] [292] [293] [294] [295]

    There were 50 diabetes-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of regulation of vasculature development, a biological program that governs the formation, patterning, maturation, and remodeling of blood vessels and is highly relevant to diabetes because vascular dysregulation contributes directly to metabolic dysfunction and to complications affecting the retina, kidney, nerve, heart, brain, placenta, bone, and wound repair. This enrichment across 50 proteins indicates a substantial concentration of diabetes-related molecular signals within vascular developmental control, consistent with the central role of endothelial proliferation, migration, sprouting, branching, lumen formation, mural cell recruitment, vessel stabilization, and tissue-specific angiocrine communication in diabetic pathophysiology.

    To place these enriched proteins into a systems-level context, the network representation below illustrates their interaction structure and connectivity.

    The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network of these 50 proteins, together with the link to the STRING webpage for interactive inspection of the network topology and connectivity relationships.

    During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following. With that overall network context in place, the following paragraphs summarize the proteins that appear especially notable within this enriched set and discuss their possible relevance to diabetes in a cautious, evidence-based manner.

    DLL1 is among the most diabetes-relevant proteins in this list because Notch signaling is fundamentally involved in pancreatic lineage specification and endocrine cell differentiation. The reported role of DLL1 in maintaining pancreatic progenitors and regulating early pancreatic epithelial patterning suggests a direct connection to beta-cell developmental competence and, by extension, long-term insulin secretory capacity. Beyond organogenesis, DLL1 also contributes to arterial identity and endothelial responsiveness to vascular endothelial growth factor A, linking it to vascular homeostasis. This is particularly important in diabetes, where both impaired beta-cell mass and microvascular dysfunction are central pathogenic features. Dysregulated DLL1-Notch signaling could therefore plausibly contribute both to defective pancreatic cell differentiation and to diabetic vascular complications through altered endothelial behavior and angiogenic control. [296] [297]

    Whereas DLL1 and HHEX point primarily to developmental specification, PTPRM is highly relevant to diabetes because its annotated function directly intersects with insulin-responsive glucose transport. The protein promotes plasma membrane trafficking of solute carrier family two member four, also known as glucose transporter type four, the principal insulin-regulated glucose transporter in adipose tissue and muscle. Impaired glucose transporter type four translocation is a core molecular defect in insulin resistance and type two diabetes. In this context, PTPRM may influence systemic glucose disposal by modulating adipocyte differentiation and preserving efficient glucose uptake machinery. Its effects on cell-cell adhesion and catenin phosphorylation also suggest broader roles in adipose tissue architecture and metabolic signaling. Among the proteins listed, PTPRM is especially notable because the mechanistic link to diabetes is immediate and centered on one of the defining biochemical abnormalities of the disease: defective peripheral glucose uptake. [192] [193] [194]

    Extending from glucose transport to endothelial regulation, AMOT is of particular interest in diabetes because it integrates endothelial barrier function with Hippo and yes associated protein one signaling, two processes increasingly implicated in diabetic complications and metabolic tissue remodeling. Diabetes is characterized by chronic endothelial dysfunction, altered vascular permeability, and abnormal angiogenic responses, especially in the retina, kidney, and wound microenvironment. AMOT may influence these processes by controlling tight junction stability and endothelial migration. Its repression of yes associated protein one and tafazzin is also noteworthy, since this signaling affects cell survival, regeneration, fibrosis, and potentially beta-cell adaptive responses. Therefore, AMOT may be relevant not only to diabetic microvascular disease but also to tissue remodeling in organs exposed to glucotoxicity and inflammation. [301]

    A related aspect of vascular remodeling involves extracellular matrix turnover, which makes CEMIP2 relevant to diabetes because extracellular matrix remodeling and hyaluronan turnover are increasingly recognized as contributors to insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, impaired wound healing, and diabetic cardiovascular disease. Hyaluronan accumulation is frequently observed in inflamed and fibrotic tissues, including adipose tissue and diabetic wounds, where it alters leukocyte recruitment, tissue stiffness, and repair responses. By degrading high-molecular-weight hyaluronan and influencing focal adhesion dynamics, CEMIP2 may shape cell migration and angiogenesis in metabolically stressed tissues. Its reported connection to vascular endothelial growth factor signaling further supports a role in diabetic vascular pathology, where abnormal angiogenesis and matrix remodeling are central features. [302] [303] [304] [305] [306]

    In parallel with matrix remodeling, inflammatory regulation is also likely to be important, and CHI3L1 is notable because it links inflammation, macrophage polarization, epithelial stress responses, and tissue remodeling, all of which are highly relevant to diabetes pathogenesis and its complications. Chronic low-grade inflammation is a hallmark of insulin resistance, and macrophage functional states in adipose tissue strongly influence metabolic homeostasis. The ability of CHI3L1 to promote M2 macrophage differentiation, modulate dendritic cell accumulation, and activate protein kinase B one and interleukin eight signaling suggests that it could shape inflammatory microenvironments in obesity, diabetic wounds, and end-organ injury. In addition, its role in tissue remodeling may connect it to fibrosis and extracellular matrix changes observed in diabetic nephropathy and other chronic complications. Thus, CHI3L1 is important primarily as an immunometabolic and remodeling-associated mediator.

    Consistent with this vascular-inflammatory interface, GDF2 is highly pertinent to diabetes because vascular integrity and endothelial signaling are central determinants of diabetic complications. The protein regulates angiogenesis and vessel stability and signals through the bone morphogenetic protein and transforming growth factor beta axis, pathways that are strongly implicated in endothelial homeostasis, inflammation, and fibrosis. In diabetes, persistent hyperglycemia disrupts endothelial function and promotes both excessive and insufficient angiogenesis depending on tissue context, such as proliferative retinopathy versus impaired wound repair. Because GDF2 supports normal vascular structure and modulates mothers against decapentaplegic homolog signaling, altered GDF2 activity could contribute to the vascular fragility, maladaptive remodeling, and organ-specific microangiopathy that define advanced diabetic disease. [49] [50] [51] [52]

    Along similar lines, HRG stands out because it sits at the intersection of inflammation, coagulation, endothelial signaling, and angiogenesis, all of which are profoundly altered in diabetes. Diabetic vasculopathy is characterized not only by endothelial dysfunction but also by a prothrombotic state, chronic sterile inflammation, and impaired resolution of tissue injury. HRG can modulate necrotic cell clearance, vascular endothelial growth factor signaling, macrophage polarization, and endothelial motility, suggesting potential relevance to diabetic wound healing, atherosclerosis, nephropathy, and retinopathy. Its heparan sulfate-dependent interactions are also notable because the endothelial glycocalyx is disrupted in diabetes. Accordingly, HRG may influence both vascular injury responses and inflammatory homeostasis in diabetic tissues.

    This convergence of inflammation and repair is also reflected in MDK, which is one of the most compelling proteins in this list for diabetes-related biology because it combines pro-inflammatory, pro-survival, pro-angiogenic, and tissue-repair functions. Diabetes involves chronic inflammation together with defective regenerative responses, especially in the vasculature, kidney, peripheral nerves, and skin. MDK recruits inflammatory cells, influences dendritic cell and T-cell responses, and activates mitogen-activated protein kinase and protein kinase B signaling, all of which could contribute to metabolic inflammation. At the same time, its ability to induce vascular endothelial growth factor A, promote endothelial proliferation, and support tissue regeneration links it to diabetic wound healing and vascular remodeling. This dual role is particularly relevant in diabetes, where excessive inflammation coexists with inadequate repair. MDK may therefore act as a context-dependent mediator of both compensatory regeneration and pathological remodeling. [307] [308] [309] [310] [311] [312] [313] [314] [315] [316]

    At the center of several of these observations is vascular endothelial growth factor-driven endothelial signaling. Regardless of the apparent annotation inconsistency in the source description, the listed functions clearly correspond to a central vascular endothelial growth factor-driven endothelial signaling axis that is highly relevant to diabetes. Diabetes-associated complications are fundamentally vascular, involving altered permeability, aberrant angiogenesis, endothelial dysfunction, and impaired nitric oxide bioavailability. A protein controlling vascular endothelial growth factor-dependent endothelial migration, survival, cytoskeletal remodeling, and nitric oxide signaling would therefore be directly implicated in diabetic retinopathy, nephropathy, macrovascular disease, and poor wound healing. This entry is especially important because it captures the convergence of vascular endothelial growth factor signaling and endothelial nitric oxide pathways, both of which are repeatedly dysregulated in hyperglycemic states.

    In a related anti-angiogenic context, SERPINF1 is particularly relevant to diabetes because anti-angiogenic balance is a major determinant of diabetic microvascular disease, especially retinopathy. A potent endogenous inhibitor of angiogenesis could modulate pathological neovascularization, which is a defining feature of proliferative diabetic retinopathy. Its neurotrophic activity is also noteworthy because diabetic neuropathy involves both vascular and neuronal injury. Therefore, SERPINF1 may be important at the interface of neurovascular protection, potentially influencing retinal integrity, peripheral nerve health, and tissue responses to chronic metabolic stress.

    Beyond angiogenic balance alone, developmental signaling pathways may also intersect with diabetic remodeling, and SFRP1 is relevant to diabetes because Wnt signaling is increasingly implicated in adipogenesis, insulin sensitivity, pancreatic development, fibrosis, and vascular remodeling. By antagonizing beta-catenin-dependent signaling, SFRP1 may influence adipose tissue expansion and differentiation, processes tightly linked to systemic insulin resistance. Its effects on vascular cell proliferation and angiogenesis further connect it to diabetic vasculopathy. In addition, Wnt pathway dysregulation has been associated with beta-cell dysfunction and diabetic kidney disease, making SFRP1 a plausible modulator of multiple disease mechanisms rather than a single isolated pathway.

    Within this broader signaling framework, SMAD1 is important in the diabetes context because bone morphogenetic protein and mothers against decapentaplegic homolog signaling regulates vascular biology, tissue differentiation, and fibrotic remodeling. Diabetic complications, particularly nephropathy and vasculopathy, involve maladaptive transforming growth factor beta and bone morphogenetic protein pathway activity. Since SMAD1 is a core effector of bone morphogenetic protein signaling and is also linked in this list to GDF2 and bone morphogenetic protein nine-related endothelial regulation, it may represent a mechanistic bridge between developmental signaling and adult vascular homeostasis. Dysregulated SMAD1 activity could contribute to altered endothelial function, tissue repair responses, and fibrosis in diabetes-associated organ damage. [317] [318] [319] [320] [176]

    Another extracellular matrix-associated factor, SMOC2, is relevant to diabetes because extracellular matrix remodeling and angiogenesis are central to both chronic complications and tissue repair failure. In diabetic wounds and ischemic tissues, defective endothelial migration and abnormal matrix organization impair healing. Conversely, in the retina and kidney, excessive or maladaptive vascular responses can drive pathology. By promoting matrix assembly and endothelial proliferation and migration, SMOC2 may influence how diabetic tissues respond to injury and vascular stress. Its role is therefore most relevant to diabetic microvascular remodeling and wound healing biology.

    This emphasis on endothelial signaling is reinforced by another entry that appears to capture the core vascular endothelial growth factor signaling machinery central to diabetes complications, notwithstanding the probable naming inconsistency in the source annotation. Vascular endothelial growth factor pathway activation is one of the most important drivers of diabetic retinopathy, contributes to glomerular injury in diabetic nephropathy, and also influences wound healing and vascular permeability. The listed functions, including endothelial survival, migration, permeability control, and nitric oxide-related responses, map directly onto known mechanisms of diabetic microangiopathy. For this reason, this protein entry is among the most clinically relevant in the set, particularly for understanding retinal neovascularization, albuminuric kidney disease, and impaired vascular repair.

    Moving from signaling to matrix-associated restraint, ANGPTL7 is not a classic diabetes gene, but it is potentially relevant because extracellular matrix deposition and angiogenic restraint are recurring themes in diabetic complications. Matrix accumulation is central to diabetic fibrosis in organs such as the kidney, while dysregulated angiogenesis contributes to retinopathy and impaired tissue repair. The described role of ANGPTL7 in matrix deposition suggests a possible link to glucocorticoid-responsive remodeling processes, which may intersect with steroid-induced diabetes or with extracellular matrix changes under metabolic stress. Its anti-angiogenic function may also be informative in the broader context of diabetes-associated vascular imbalance. [321] [322]

    Consistent with that remodeling perspective, BMPER is potentially relevant to diabetes through its modulation of bone morphogenetic protein signaling, a pathway involved not only in skeletal biology but also in vascular homeostasis, adipose biology, and tissue remodeling. Although the annotation emphasizes osteoblasts and chondrocytes, bone morphogenetic protein pathway regulation can influence systemic metabolism and diabetic complication phenotypes, especially where calcification, fibrosis, or altered repair responses are present. Thus, BMPER may be a secondary but mechanistically plausible contributor to diabetes-related tissue remodeling.

    From tissue remodeling, the discussion naturally extends to cardiovascular adaptation, and HSPB6 is relevant to diabetes because cardiovascular dysfunction is a major cause of morbidity in diabetic patients. Its roles in vasorelaxation, cardiac contractility, cardioprotection, and post-injury angiogenesis suggest that it may modulate the response of the diabetic heart and vasculature to metabolic and oxidative stress. Since diabetes is associated with endothelial dysfunction, impaired vasodilation, and diabetic cardiomyopathy, a chaperone that supports vascular relaxation and tissue protection after injury could have substantial pathophysiological significance.

    A related matrix-centered consideration applies to HYAL1, which has a plausible connection to diabetes through extracellular matrix and hyaluronan turnover. Hyaluronan metabolism affects inflammation, fibrosis, vascular permeability, and wound repair, all of which are altered in diabetes. Although the annotation here is limited, enzymes that remodel hyaluronan can influence tissue stiffness, immune cell trafficking, and healing outcomes, suggesting potential relevance to diabetic nephropathy, skin ulcers, and adipose tissue inflammation.

    Finally, GRN may be relevant to diabetes through lysosomal function and proteostasis. Lysosomal dysfunction has emerged as an important feature of metabolic disease, influencing inflammation, lipid handling, autophagy, and beta-cell stress responses. By stabilizing cathepsin D, GRN could affect protein turnover and inflammatory signaling in metabolically active tissues. Although the diabetes connection is indirect based on the present annotation, GRN is noteworthy because disturbances in lysosomal biology contribute to insulin resistance and diabetic organ injury.

    7. Complement system (WP:WP2806)

    Agent Summary: The complement system, a crucial component of innate immunity, involves various pathways that converge on the cleavage of complement component three, leading to the generation of effector fragments that play roles in inflammation, opsonization, and cell injury Core family members: C2, C3, C7, C9, CFB, CFH. Context proteins (upstream regulators / disease context, not direct members): CALCA. [248] [249] [250]
    Read Context ▽

    The complement system is a central arm of innate immunity composed of soluble plasma proteins, membrane-associated receptors, and regulatory factors that together detect danger, amplify inflammatory signaling, opsonize targets for phagocytosis, recruit leukocytes, and directly injure susceptible cells through membrane attack complex formation. Complement activation proceeds through the classical pathway, the lectin pathway, and the alternative pathway, all of which converge on cleavage of complement component three, followed by generation of downstream effector fragments such as complement component three a, complement component five a, and terminal complement complexes. Beyond host defense against infection, the complement system has major homeostatic functions in immune complex clearance, apoptotic cell disposal, shaping of adaptive immunity, tissue remodeling, and metabolic regulation. Tight regulation is essential because excessive or misplaced activation can produce chronic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, thrombogenicity, and parenchymal injury. Recent work further indicates that complement is not only liver-derived and circulating, but can also be produced and activated locally within tissues and even intracellularly, where it influences cellular metabolism, transcriptional programs, autophagy, inflammatory tone, fibrosis, and repair. This broader biological scope makes the complement system highly relevant to chronic metabolic disease, including autoimmune beta cell destruction, insulin resistance, diabetic kidney disease, diabetic retinal disease, and neurocognitive complications associated with diabetes.

    Against this biological background, the collected literature suggests that the complement system is related to diabetes at multiple stages of disease initiation, progression, and complication development. In type one diabetes, complement appears to participate in autoimmune susceptibility and early disease evolution. Genetic studies implicate variation linked to complement component four a and complement component four b in differential risk within the human leukocyte antigen region, suggesting that complement-related immune regulation may modify disease predisposition and endotype structure, particularly in individuals whose first autoantibody targets insulin [248]. Additional studies indicate that disruption of complement biology may precede clinical disease, because children who later develop islet autoimmunity and progress to type one diabetes exhibit reduced levels of multiple complement proteins before autoantibody detection and through disease onset, supporting complement proteins as early biomarkers and possible mechanistic participants in beta cell autoimmunity [249]. This interpretation is further supported by glycomic and genetic evidence linking complement component three variation and altered glycosylation to recent-onset type one diabetes, implying that complement structure and activation state may influence inflammatory potential and disease susceptibility [250] [251].

    A related but broader pattern is described in type two diabetes, where the association appears to extend more strongly into metabolic dysfunction. Reviews and clinical studies describe complement activation as a feature of obesity, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and hyperglycemia, with circulating complement component one q, complement component three, complement component four, complement factor h, and complement component three b associated with glycemic control, lipid abnormalities, beta cell function, and insulin resistance, and with evidence suggesting that the alternative pathway may be particularly relevant in type two diabetes [252] [253] [254]. Complement-related adipokines may also contribute to metabolic risk, as Mendelian randomization suggested a possible causal role of adipsin in type two diabetes and causal effects of inflammatory mediators on insulin sensitivity and beta cell function in African populations [255].

    This metabolic and inflammatory framework becomes especially important when considering diabetic complications, where the translational evidence appears strongest. Diabetic kidney disease is particularly well supported, as urinary complement proteins including complement component two, complement component five a, collectin kidney one, complement component six, complement factor h, and complement component seven robustly predict progression to kidney failure in both type one and type two diabetes, while kidney tissue studies demonstrate increased complement protein abundance and local expression within diseased diabetic kidneys [256]. Consistently, glomerular deposition of complement component four c in biopsy-proven diabetic kidney disease is associated with heavier proteinuria, more inflammation, and faster progression to end-stage kidney disease, identifying complement activation as a marker and likely mediator of renal injury [257]. Broader kidney literature further supports a pathogenic role for local complement activation in fibrosis and chronic kidney disease progression, which is highly relevant to diabetic nephropathy [258] [259]. Complement dysregulation has also been linked to diabetic retinal disease and to cognitive impairment in diabetes, including elevated complement proteins in astrocyte-derived exosomes from people with type one diabetes and mild cognitive impairment, suggesting that complement-mediated neuroinflammation may contribute to extra-renal diabetic complications [260] [261]. Taken together, the available evidence supports the view that the complement system may represent more than a bystander in diabetes, instead plausibly acting as a mechanistic bridge between innate immunity, autoimmunity, metabolism, inflammation, and tissue injury across both major forms of diabetes and their chronic complications. [248] [262] [256] [253] [255] [260] [257] [263] [264] [258] [252] [250] [249] [254] [259] [251] [261]

    Consistent with this literature context, there were 25 diabetes-associated proteins significantly enriched in the complement system pathway, a core innate immune program that integrates soluble plasma proteins, membrane-associated receptors, and regulatory factors to detect danger signals, amplify inflammation, promote opsonization, recruit leukocytes, and induce target cell injury through terminal complement complex formation. Enrichment across 25 proteins suggests a substantial concentration of diabetes-related molecular signals within a single immunometabolic pathway, which is in line with the broad contribution of complement activation to autoimmune beta cell injury, insulin resistance, diabetic kidney disease, diabetic retinal disease, and neurocognitive complications associated with diabetes. The pathway biology is quantitatively notable because it spans 3 major activation routes, namely the classical pathway, the lectin pathway, and the alternative pathway, which converge on complement component three cleavage and subsequently generate multiple downstream effector fragments, including complement component three a, complement component five a, and terminal complement complexes. In the context of diabetes, the enrichment of 25 proteins in this pathway supports the interpretation that dysregulated complement activity may contribute not only to host defense imbalance, but also to chronic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, thrombogenicity, tissue remodeling, fibrosis, and altered metabolic regulation.

    To further contextualize this enrichment, the figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network for these 25 enriched proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for interactive exploration of the network topology and functional connectivity.

    ADIPOQ is the most directly relevant protein in this set with respect to diabetes because it encodes adiponectin, a canonical adipokine that links adipose tissue biology to systemic glucose and lipid homeostasis. The reported activation of adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase and protein kinase B is particularly important, as these pathways are central regulators of insulin sensitivity, glucose uptake, fatty acid oxidation, and metabolic stress responses. In the context of type two diabetes, reduced adiponectin signaling is strongly associated with insulin resistance, ectopic lipid accumulation, and chronic low-grade inflammation. Therefore, a protein whose core function is to stimulate adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase and protein kinase B signaling stands out as mechanistically connected to improved metabolic control and protection from diabetic pathology. Its additional engagement of mitogen-activated protein kinase suggests broader effects on cell survival and metabolic adaptation. Overall, ADIPOQ is highly relevant because dysfunction in adipokine signaling is a major feature of obesity-associated diabetes, and adiponectin is widely regarded as a protective endocrine factor in this disease setting.

    In a related but distinct way, ADM appears relevant to diabetes primarily through its vascular and metabolic implications. Although the provided function emphasizes receptor usage rather than a specific diabetic phenotype, adrenomedullin signaling is notable because diabetes is characterized not only by disordered glucose metabolism but also by endothelial dysfunction, altered tissue perfusion, and progressive microvascular injury. A ligand with defined activity through calcitonin receptor-like receptor and receptor activity-modifying protein receptor complexes may influence vascular tone, endothelial integrity, and tissue stress responses, all of which are highly pertinent to diabetic complications such as nephropathy, retinopathy, and cardiovascular disease. ADM therefore stands out as a potential mediator at the interface between metabolic disease and vascular adaptation. Its importance may be greater in the complication phase of diabetes than in primary insulin resistance, but this still makes it biologically meaningful across the broader diabetic disease spectrum.

    Extending from vascular adaptation to extracellular remodeling, PLAUR is of interest in diabetes because it connects extracellular proteolysis, cell-surface signaling, and tissue remodeling, processes that are frequently dysregulated in chronic diabetic states. Its role in localizing urokinase activity and promoting plasmin formation suggests involvement in matrix turnover, inflammatory cell migration, and wound repair. These functions are especially relevant to diabetes, where impaired tissue remodeling and defective healing are common clinical problems, particularly in the skin, vasculature, and kidney. In addition, the proteolysis-independent signaling functions of PLAUR imply that it may influence inflammatory or stress-response pathways beyond matrix degradation alone. This is important because diabetes is increasingly understood as a disease of both metabolic dysfunction and maladaptive inflammation. Thus, PLAUR may be mechanistically linked to diabetic complications through altered extracellular matrix dynamics, inflammation, and repair processes. [265]

    Finally, LAMB1 is less directly connected to core glucose homeostasis than ADIPOQ, but it remains potentially relevant to diabetes because basement membrane structure and extracellular matrix organization are central to diabetic tissue injury. The described role of LAMB1 in cell attachment, migration, and maintenance of basement membrane integrity suggests a broader importance in preserving tissue architecture. In diabetes, excessive extracellular matrix remodeling and basement membrane thickening are hallmark features of microvascular complications, particularly in the kidney and retina. A laminin subunit involved in structural organization may therefore contribute to susceptibility or response to diabetic damage, even if the provided functional description is framed mainly in developmental and neuroarchitectural terms. Its relevance is thus likely indirect but still meaningful, especially in relation to chronic tissue remodeling and barrier dysfunction in diabetic complications.

    8. Pluripotent stem cell differentiation pathway (WP:WP2848)

    Agent Summary: The pluripotent stem cell differentiation pathway is crucial for understanding the development of insulin-producing beta cells from pluripotent stem cells, which is relevant for diabetes treatment. Pathway members (enrichment overlap): BMP4, CSF1, CSF1R, EPO, FLT3LG, HGF. Context proteins (upstream regulators / disease context, not direct members): BMP6, NOS3, NTRK3. [217] [218] [219]
    Read Context ▽

    The pluripotent stem cell differentiation pathway describes the molecular and cellular program through which pluripotent stem cells, including embryonic stem cells and induced pluripotent stem cells, exit self-renewal and progressively acquire specialized identities. In the context of pancreatic development, this pathway is especially important because it recapitulates the sequential transitions from pluripotency to definitive endoderm, primitive gut tube, pancreatic progenitor, endocrine progenitor, and finally insulin-producing beta-like cells and islet-like structures. This process is controlled by tightly coordinated transcriptional regulators, extracellular matrix signals, and developmental signaling pathways, including wingless-related integration site signaling, bone morphogenetic protein signaling, c-Jun N-terminal kinase signaling, and lineage-defining factors such as forkhead box A2 and neurogenin 3. Studies of human pluripotent stem cell differentiation have shown that endocrine and progenitor compartments emerge as distinct cellular states during in vitro pancreatic specification, and that precise modulation of signaling intensity and timing is required to favor endocrine commitment over alternative fates. In addition, the local pancreatic microenvironment, including mesenchymal and endothelial cues, strongly influences beta-cell differentiation and maturation, while three-dimensional culture systems and biomaterial scaffolds improve structural organization and glucose-responsive insulin secretion. Thus, the pluripotent stem cell differentiation pathway is not only a developmental program but also a translational framework for generating replacement beta cells, modeling diabetes-associated defects in endocrine development and insulin action, and identifying barriers to safe and effective regenerative therapy.

    To complement this enrichment result, the interaction network below provides a visual summary of the relationships among these proteins and offers an additional layer for interpretation.

    The figure below shows the protein-protein interaction network of these 15 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for interactive inspection.

    Following this network-level overview, the enriched proteins can be considered individually to clarify how each may contribute to diabetes-related mechanisms. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

    Among the listed proteins, BMP4 stands out because its signaling profile intersects with several biological processes that are highly relevant to diabetes, particularly vascular dysfunction, tissue remodeling, and metabolic stress responses. Diabetes is characterized not only by impaired glucose homeostasis but also by progressive microvascular and macrovascular injury, defective wound healing, and altered tissue repair. BMP4 is notable in this context because it regulates vascular development and angiogenesis and can activate both canonical SMAD-dependent pathways and non-canonical signaling routes, including phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase and protein kinase B and SRC, which are central to endothelial survival and vascular adaptation. Particularly relevant is the observation that BMP4 can induce SRC phosphorylation and activate vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2, linking it mechanistically to pro-angiogenic signaling. This is important for diabetic complications such as retinopathy, nephropathy, and impaired wound healing, where abnormal angiogenesis and endothelial dysfunction are major pathogenic features. In addition, BMP4 belongs to a broader signaling family that has been implicated in inflammation, fibrosis, and vascular calcification, all of which are common in diabetes. Thus, even though the provided annotation emphasizes developmental biology, the vascular and signaling functions of BMP4 may make it a plausible contributor to diabetes-associated endothelial injury and maladaptive angiogenic remodeling. [173] [174] [175] [176] [177] [178] [179]

    In a related way, NOTCH1 may also connect developmental regulation with vascular pathology in diabetes. NOTCH1 is highly relevant to diabetes because it integrates cell-fate control with vascular homeostasis, two processes that are deeply disturbed in diabetic disease. The most compelling diabetes-related aspect of NOTCH1 in the provided annotation is its role in angiogenesis, specifically its ability to negatively regulate endothelial proliferation, migration, and sprouting. This is directly pertinent to diabetic microvascular complications, where endothelial dysfunction, aberrant angiogenesis, and impaired vascular repair are central mechanisms. For example, diabetic retinopathy involves pathological neovascular responses, whereas diabetic wound healing is marked by insufficient or dysregulated vessel formation; altered NOTCH1 signaling could plausibly contribute to both settings by changing the balance between quiescent and activated endothelial states. Beyond vasculature, NOTCH1 governs differentiation, proliferation, and apoptosis, processes that are also relevant to pancreatic tissue remodeling, immune regulation, and fibrosis in diabetes. Its broader developmental and cell-specification roles further support the view that dysregulated NOTCH signaling may influence tissue adaptation under chronic hyperglycemic stress. Therefore, NOTCH1 stands out as a strong candidate linking diabetes to abnormal endothelial behavior and defective tissue repair.

    Extending this perspective from signaling control to extracellular metabolic regulation, NT5E may be relevant through its effects on the local inflammatory and vascular environment. NT5E is potentially relevant to diabetes because it is a key regulator of extracellular nucleotide metabolism, particularly through the conversion of adenosine monophosphate to adenosine. Although the provided annotation is primarily enzymatic, this function has important pathophysiological implications. Extracellular adenosine is a major signaling molecule that modulates inflammation, vascular tone, endothelial barrier function, and tissue protection during metabolic stress. These processes are highly relevant to diabetes, where chronic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, ischemia, and altered tissue perfusion contribute to complications in the kidney, retina, heart, and peripheral tissues. By shaping the extracellular balance between pro-inflammatory nucleotides and anti-inflammatory or vasoregulatory nucleosides, NT5E may influence the local tissue environment in diabetes. Its ability to hydrolyze nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide and nicotinamide mononucleotide is also noteworthy because these metabolites are linked to cellular energy homeostasis and redox biology, both of which are disrupted in diabetes. Therefore, while NT5E is not a classic diabetes gene in this list, its metabolic and purinergic regulatory functions may make it mechanistically relevant to diabetic vascular injury and chronic inflammatory stress. [225]

    From extracellular metabolism, the analysis then shifts to coagulation biology, which is also central to diabetic complications. TF is particularly important in diabetes because hypercoagulability and thrombo-inflammatory activation are hallmarks of the diabetic state. The core function of TF as the initiator of the extrinsic coagulation cascade makes it directly relevant to the increased risk of atherothrombosis, myocardial infarction, stroke, and microvascular occlusion observed in patients with diabetes. In diabetic tissues, endothelial injury, inflammation, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysfunction can promote a prothrombotic environment, and TF is a central molecular trigger of this response. Its capacity to activate factors nine and ten through the TF:factor seven a complex places it at the apex of coagulation initiation, meaning that dysregulation of TF expression or activity can have amplified downstream effects on thrombin generation and fibrin formation. This is especially meaningful in diabetes, where coagulation abnormalities intersect with vascular inflammation and endothelial dysfunction to accelerate cardiovascular complications. Accordingly, TF stands out as one of the most clinically relevant proteins in the list because it connects diabetes to one of its most serious outcomes: heightened thrombotic risk.

    Finally, VEGFA provides perhaps the clearest bridge between the enriched pathway and the vascular complications that dominate diabetes morbidity. VEGFA is arguably the most directly diabetes-relevant protein in the list because its annotated functions map closely onto the vascular abnormalities that define many diabetic complications. Its central roles in angiogenesis, vascular permeability, endothelial survival, migration, and nitric oxide signaling are especially important in diabetic retinopathy, diabetic nephropathy, and impaired wound healing. In diabetic retinopathy, excessive vascular endothelial growth factor pathway activation is strongly associated with pathological neovascularization and increased vascular permeability, leading to retinal edema and vision loss. The annotation also emphasizes activation of protein kinase B, mitogen-activated protein kinase and extracellular signal-regulated kinase, SRC, focal adhesion kinase, and nitric oxide synthase pathways, all of which are critical mediators of endothelial responses to injury and metabolic stress. These signaling outputs are highly relevant to diabetes, where chronic hyperglycemia disrupts endothelial homeostasis, impairs nitric oxide bioavailability, and promotes abnormal vessel remodeling. The mention of isoforms that can act as decoy receptors is also notable, as it suggests a built-in regulatory mechanism that may influence the balance between physiological and pathological angiogenesis. Overall, VEGFA stands out as a major mechanistic and clinical link to diabetes because it directly governs the vascular leakage, aberrant angiogenesis, and endothelial dysfunction that underlie several of the most consequential diabetic complications.
